outcome: The upper-bound side (Huxley's 131/416 ≈ 0.3149 exponent for Δ(x)=O(x^θ+ε)) has not moved in the window: a claimed improvement to θ≈0.314483 by Li and Yang has existed as an arXiv preprint since August 2023 (before the frozen revision) and remains unpublished and undigested as of September 2026, so it does not count as a change. But the lower-bound (Ω) side of the classical k=1 problem did move in the window: Sourmelidis (arXiv:2411.14221, Nov 2024, accepted at Mathematika) and Mahatab (arXiv:2504.17032, Apr 2025, published in the Ramanujan Journal, 2026) independently improved Soundararajan's 2003 Ω-result for Δ(x) using the resonance method, and Lamzouri (arXiv:2605.21476, May 2026) then obtained a further, conjecturally sharp Ω+ result removing a log-loss factor that had persisted since Hafner's 1981 bound — the paper's own abstract calls it 'the first improvement on Hafner's 1981 Ω+ result for the divisor problem.' These are genuine, peer-reviewed advances specifically on the classical (k=1) case, so the problem counts as partial progress, not open-with-no-change.

disputes.summary: Sourmelidis's improvement to Soundararajan's omega result and Mahatab's improvement were obtained independently using different resonator constructions; Mahatab's paper states the two efforts were concurrent and independent, with no priority conflict claimed by either side.

summary: The k=1 (classical Dirichlet) divisor problem has two live fronts: the upper bound on θ in Δ(x)=O(x^θ+ε), and the omega (lower bound / oscillation) side showing Δ(x) must be at least as large as some function infinitely often. On the upper-bound side, the triage record surfaced a Feb 2025 UIUC talk by Xuerui Yang and Xiaochun Li reporting θ≈0.314483, beating Huxley's 131/416≈0.31490. I traced this to arXiv:2308.14859, whose v1 was posted 28 August 2023 and v2 on 14 September 2023 — both before the 26 January 2024 frozen-revision cutoff. I checked Yang's own personal site listing her publications: as of the check, this paper is still listed as a 'preprint' with no journal, more than two years after posting, and the current (September 2026) Wikipedia article on the divisor summatory function still cites only Huxley's 2003 bound as the record, not Li-Yang's. There is no dated post-window re-submission, correction, or expert digestion (no Bulletin/Annals writeup, no blog digestion by e.g. Tao) that I could find. So this claim is excluded from the window under §6.3 (dated by first written argument, which predates the cutoff) and also fails the `resolved`/`claimed` bar since no expert has published a check of it. On the omega side, which is squarely the k=1 case and not a variant, three papers moved the bound within the window: Sourmelidis (arXiv:2411.14221, submitted 21 Nov 2024, revised 29 Apr 2026, noted as 'to appear in Mathematika' with an active DOI) and Mahatab (arXiv:2504.17032, submitted 23 Apr 2025, published in the Ramanujan Journal vol. 69, article 91, 2026) independently improved Soundararajan's 2003 omega result via the resonance method; Lamzouri (arXiv:2605.21476, submitted 20 May 2026) then sharpened this further, explicitly billing it as the first improvement on Hafner's 1981 Ω+ bound. None of these papers' abstracts, and none of the secondary summaries I could extract, mention any AI or machine-learning tool in deriving the mathematics. Overall: `partial` progress, `ai_role` none, dated to the first (Sourmelidis) preprint in the chain, 21 November 2024.
competing_reading: One could argue the omega-side improvements are a 'related' refinement rather than a case of 'the' problem, since Wikipedia's bullet (as commonly read) is usually about the upper-bound exponent θ, and the omega side is a different (though classical and well-established) sub-question about the same Δ(x). I read it as squarely in scope because the Piltz/Dirichlet divisor problem is standardly understood to include both the upper- and lower-bound sides of Δ(x)'s growth, and Wikipedia's own phrasing ('bounding Δ_k(x)') does not restrict to one direction. If a stricter reading confines the bullet to only the upper bound (θ), the correct status would be `open` with `no_change_found` true, since the Li-Yang claim is pre-window and undigested.
what_would_settle_it: A clear statement, e.g. in the Wikipedia article's own wording or a canonical survey, of whether the bullet is meant to cover only the upper bound θ or both directions of Δ(x)'s growth. Also, any future journal acceptance or expert digestion (e.g., a referee report, a citation as an established result in a survey, or a Tao-style blog write-up) of the Li-Yang 2023 preprint would settle whether the upper-bound side has genuinely moved, and would push that event's classification toward `open_stale` (since dated pre-window) rather than remaining excluded as unverified.

dead_ends: Could not find any MathOverflow, blog (Tao or otherwise), or journal digestion confirming or disputing the Li-Yang 2023 preprint's correctness — it appears to sit unreviewed rather than actively disputed.

The live Wikipedia article on the divisor summatory function does not mention the Li-Yang result at all, which is weak secondary evidence it hasn't been accepted by the community, but is not conclusive.

PDF text extraction via WebFetch on the UIUC talk slides and the Li-Yang paper itself was not fully reliable (binary/compressed stream issues), so I relied on search-engine summaries and secondary citations for some numeric details; I was not able to independently re-derive or directly quote the 0.314483 figure from the primary PDF text.

incomplete: I could not directly extract readable text from the arXiv PDF (2308.14859) or the UIUC talk slides via automated fetch (both returned binary/compressed stream content), so the exact numeric exponent (0.314483) and any acknowledgements section are taken from secondary search-engine summaries rather than a direct read of the primary text. I also could not find independent confirmation of whether the Li-Yang preprint has been submitted to or rejected by any journal, only that it remains listed as an unpublished preprint. These gaps affect confidence on the upper-bound side but not on the omega-side chain (Sourmelidis/Mahatab/Lamzouri), which I was able to verify via readable abstracts, submission-history pages, and a live journal DOI.

judgement.doubts: The bullet asks about bounding Δ(x); the question stays open, so Ω-improvements are bounds, not a settled case. All three post-snapshot Ω events are in the same progress tier and all have ai_role none; the recorded event (Sourmelidis) is kept. The bullet's 'k = 1' is Wikipedia's indexing quirk (classical case is usually k=2); it does not change the reading. Li-Yang's pre-snapshot upper bound is also only a bound, so it could never have made this open_stale.
